title: Edmonton South Asians finalize plans with city for central Diwali festival
excerpt: After October 2025 Diwali fireworks sparked fires and a wave of hate, South Asian leaders and the City of Edmonton are finalizing a Canada Day-style central celebration at Mill Woods Park, with permits pending and details expected within weeks.
body:
• Edmonton's South Asian leaders and the city are finalizing plans for a central Diwali festival at Mill Woods Park, modeled on Canada Day celebrations.
  • The push follows October 2025, when Diwali fireworks sparked multiple fires — including a $175,000 house fire and three arson charges — and organizers say the backlash fueled a surge in hate toward the community.
  • Plans call for early-evening fireworks launched across the park's pond in the cricket field; event and fireworks permits still need approval, with Edmonton Fire Rescue aiming to settle details in about two weeks.
  • Organizers say the festival would be open to all Edmontonians — a safe, shared celebration rather than scattered backyard displays.

EDMONTON — About two months before Diwali lights up the night sky, Edmonton's South Asian community leaders are working with the city to finalize plans for a central Diwali festival at Mill Woods Park — a Canada Day-style celebration meant to replace the scattered backyard fireworks displays that turned last year's festival into a crisis.

Sunny Kakar and Raj Malhotra, co-chairs of the Sifarish Network, a group that connects the South Asian community with others in the city, said they have been in discussions with the city throughout the summer. Details are still being finalized, but the plan centers on a full festival at Mill Woods Park with fireworks set off early in the evening and launched across the pond in the cricket field.

"We don't want this celebration that's so important to so many of us have angst around it. We want the entire community, to celebrate together and do so safely."

— Sunny Kakar, co-chair, Sifarish Network

Context & Background

Last year's Diwali celebrations in Edmonton were marred by multiple fires believed to have been caused by fireworks. A house at 25 Avenue and 24 Street in the Silverberry neighbourhood was damaged in October 2025. Edmonton fire services fielded 60 calls reporting illegal fireworks, and one home suffered about $175,000 in damage after illegal fireworks ignited it.

In the Mill Woods area, a family's garage was struck by fireworks launched from a neighbouring yard on Oct. 20, 2025, destroying the garage and a recently purchased vehicle; three adult men were later charged with arson for recklessly causing damage by fire or explosion. The homeowner behind a GoFundMe that raised over $13,000 from 267 donors called for tougher penalties, and Edmonton police reminded residents that fireworks are not permitted within city limits without a permit: "No permit. No fireworks. Light up your home, not your neighbour's roof."

The fallout extended beyond property damage. Kakar and Malhotra say the fires triggered a massive increase in hate directed at the South Asian community. A city councillor, Keren Tang, pushed for stricter rules around fireworks after two houses caught fire, and CityNews reported this summer that the city was exploring running its own Diwali festival with a fireworks show.

Edmonton already hosts a large community Diwali event: Chamak Diwali 2025, held Oct. 25 at Fan Park @ ICE District and billed as the city's biggest Diwali celebration, drew crowds with headliners including Mickey Singh, Raghav and DJ Shadow Dubai, plus food trucks and fireworks. The proposed Mill Woods festival would be different — a city-partnered, open celebration rather than a ticketed concert-style event.

Impact & Analysis

Moving the fireworks to a single, professionally run site would address two problems at once: the public-safety risk of backyard pyrotechnics in residential neighbourhoods, and the reputational damage the community absorbs when illegal displays go wrong. Organizers framed the festival as a harm-reduction strategy — giving people a better option than lighting fireworks at home.

"Our focus is to take away the people that are doing these in their homes, and we want to bring them to a centralized place where we can do it in a safe manner."

— Raj Malhotra, co-chair, Sifarish Network

The venue choice is significant. Mill Woods sits in southeast Edmonton, home to one of the city's largest South Asian communities, and the park's layout — with fireworks launched across the pond in the cricket field — creates a natural buffer between the display and spectators. Staging the fireworks early in the evening also addresses a common complaint about late-night displays: noise.

Diaspora Angle

The episode illustrates how diaspora communities are learning to convert visibility into civic capital. Last year, Diwali made headlines in Edmonton for the wrong reasons — fires, fines, police warnings. Rather than retreat from public celebration, community leaders leaned in, spending the summer at the table with city officials to build an institution: a festival that treats Diwali the way Canada Day is treated — public, open to everyone, and run with the city's blessing.

The open-invitation framing is deliberate. "It wouldn't just be for the South Asian community; anyone would be able to join the festivities," the organizers said — a chance for other Edmontonians to experience the culture and "have light conquer darkness." As Kakar put it: "Let's try to not make this an occasion to spike the hate, but to make something positive out of it."

What's Next

Permits for the festival and the fireworks still need approval. Edmonton Fire Rescue told CityNews it is still working out details, which could be ready in about two weeks. That timeline leaves roughly six weeks before Diwali to lock in logistics, promotion and crowd management — tight, but workable for a single-evening event.

For now, the plan's success rests on two things: getting the permits signed, and convincing residents who have always lit fireworks in their backyards to come to the park instead. If it works, Edmonton would have a template other Canadian cities could copy — a Diwali that belongs to the whole city, not just the community that celebrates it.
